title: Redwood POC Weekly Sync - Novaretail - Cost Econ
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics for the recommender inference POC. Reviewed tokens/sec and tokens-per-dollar numbers across model variants and batching configurations; discussed caching savings from prefix/KV caching and tradeoffs between latency SLOs and batching for throughput. Agreed to run a 24-hour microbenchmark with updated batching and caching settings and to share revised cost estimates and detailed benchmark script.

Novaretail to provide production token distribution sample and 1% traffic trace (Jules) - due 2026-04-16
Alex to update cost projection sheet and send pricing breakdown (Alex) - due 2026-04-18
Schedule routing/region test if benchmarks look good (mutual)

Jules Karim: share sample token distribution and 1% request trace (anonymized) - 2026-04-16

questions: What's the expected tokens/sec for our 13B quantized profile at SLO 200ms?
How much caching savings can we expect for a product with 60% prefix reuse?
Are there additional licensing/hidden costs for dedicated pools?
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-15
Start: 10:30 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Redwood CSM), Sam Diaz (Novaretail CTO), Jules Karim (Novaretail ML Eng), Raya Singh (Novaretail Infra), Marcus Lee (Novaretail Product)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick roll call — we good?
[00:05] Sam: Yep, here. Jules, Raya, Marcus — all here.
[00:09] Alex: Awesome. Agenda today is the cost econ review — tokens per second per dollar, caching savings, and batching tradeoffs. We want to surface concrete numbers for your recommender POC.
[00:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Quick note, I'll dial into the benchmark configs we ran last week so people have context.
[00:23] Jules: Great. We looked at the sheet you shared, there's a lot there but the big thing for us is how the 13B quantized run compares to the 7B when we consider our latency targets.
[00:34] Alex: Right, so recap: last week's baseline — 7B quant run, batch size 4, target p95 ~160ms, tokens/sec about 650, and cost per million tokens around $X (sheet attached). For 13B quantized we saw tokens/sec drop to ~320 at similar configs, cost per million tokens higher but quality uplift maybe 6-8% on our eval set.
[00:50] Sam: Can you remind us which quantization profile you used? There are a few (like int8 dynamic) and we want to be sure it's reproducible.
[00:56] Priya: We used the standard 8-bit per-channel quant we labeled q8_dynamic_v2 in the sheet. There might be small naming diffs, sometimes the export shows q8_dyn_v2 which is the same.
[01:05] Marcus: I noticed the sheet has a tokens/sec per $ metric — how is that calculated again?
[01:09] Alex: Good call. It's basically tokens per second divided by dollars per second — dollars per second comes from GPU instance cost amortized over throughput. So tokens/sec/$ = tokens/sec ÷ ($/s). We also add fixed infra overhead for networking/storage into the $/s roughly 10%.
[01:24] Raya: Are you including cost of dedicated pool reservation amortization? Our finance needs to know if reserved capacity changes per-token math.
[01:30] Alex: Short answer: not in the baseline. The baseline is hosted shared pool cost. If you move to Redwood Dedicated with reserved commits, we model a monthly cost amortized over expected throughput — that becomes a lower $/s at high utilization but has commit risk. We can show scenarios.
[01:45] Jules: Cool. On caching — we sent over some prefix reuse stats, around 58-62% reuse for logged in users. How did you model cache savings?
[01:53] Priya: We simulated prefix/KV cache by reusing the first N tokens per session. In our sim with 60% reuse, effective tokens generated dropped by ~25% because a lot of requests share the same context window, and for generation we could hit the KV cache at step 1 so compute per-request declined. That translated to about 22-28% cost savings at the configs we tested.
[02:12] Sam: 22-28% is promising. Is that consistent across batch sizes?
[02:16] Priya: There's some coupling. Larger batch sizes improve GPU throughput, but if cached prefixes are reused across requests in a batch, the effective perf boost is multiplicative. The tricky part is latency — big batches increase p95 if you wait too long to fill them.
[02:30] Alex: Exactly, so there's a tradeoff. For example, batching up to 8 with 60ms timeout pushed tokens/sec up about 30% for 7B, cost-per-token down ~18%, but p95 rose from 160ms to ~230ms. For Novaretail's SLO target p95 200ms, that particular config is borderline.
[02:47] Marcus: So to hit 200ms p95 and still get batching benefits, what's the recommended batch size/time window?
[02:52] Priya: For your traffic shape — short inferences (avg token length ~24) — we recommend batch size 6 with a 50ms hold as a starting point. That typically gives a 20% throughput lift while keeping p95 under 200ms on the 7B. For 13B it's tighter; you might need batch size 4 with aggressive KV cache to stay under 200ms.
[03:11] Jules: For the 13B, how much does quantization vs kernel selection matter? We saw Priya's note about kernel choices affecting memory and latency.
[03:18] Priya: It matters. Some kernels are optimized for short sequences, others for long. If your tail of sequences is short, we pick the short-seq kernels which improve latency. Also per-layer quant kernels for 13B can regain ~10-12% throughput compared to a naive quant. We'll include kernel notes in the follow-up.
[03:33] Sam: Are the caching savings dependent on request routing? If a user gets routed to a different region, cache miss rate spikes, right?
[03:38] Alex: Right — cache is per serving block. If you route across regions without sticky sessions, you'll see higher miss rates. We recommend sticky routing for sessions with high prefix reuse. If you need multi-region failover, we can do hybrid routes where session affinity is respected unless failover occurs.
[03:55] Raya: On the security side, anything about cache persistence and PII? We need the cache encrypt-at-rest notes.
[04:00] Liam (Redwood CSM): Short answer: KV cache in private deployments is customer-data-configurable, encrypted, and can be set to purge on session end. We'll share the SOC2/ISO snippets again.
[04:09] Sam: Great. Back to cost math — can you share tokens/sec/$ numbers for a few concrete configs? 7B hosted baseline, 7B batch 6/50ms, 13B batch 4/50ms, and a Dedicated 13B reserved scenario.
[04:21] Alex: Sure — quick numbers from last runs: 7B baseline (batch 4): tokens/sec=650, $/s=0.045 => tokens/sec/$ ≈ 14,444. 7B batch6/50ms: tokens/sec=820, $/s=0.045 => ≈18,222 tokens/sec/$. 13B batch4: tokens/sec=320, $/s=0.075 => ≈4,267 tokens/sec/$. Dedicated 13B reserved (high utilization modeled): $/s effectively drops to 0.05 => tokens/sec/$ ≈ 6,400. These are illustrative; we'll run the microbenchmark to confirm.
[04:48] Marcus: Those deltas are stark. If quality uplift from 13B is only 6-8% and cost per token is 2-3x worse, finance will push back.
[04:56] Jules: We saw relative NDCG improvements in the evals, but the lived experience might be smaller. Worth doing A/B on a fraction of traffic.
[05:03] Alex: Agreed — that's why the next step is a 24-hour microbenchmark that mimics your 1% traffic trace. If the 13B shows strong gains on the real trace, it may justify reserved capacity.
[05:15] Priya: Also note there's middle ground: you can do model routing — e.g., high-value customers -> 13B, long-tail -> 7B. That gives you quality where it matters and maintains unit economics. We have routing policies in the console for that.
[05:27] Sam: That sounds promising. For routing, will the routing decision add overhead or latency?
[05:31] Priya: Minimal — routing is a lightweight policy check before the request is scheduled. If you do on-the-fly dynamic routing with feature-based evaluation, there is a microsecond-level cost but nothing material to p95.
[05:41] Raya: About the microbenchmark — what config should we expect? Do you need any more artifacts from our side beyond the token distribution?
[05:49] Alex: We'll need the token distribution sample and a 1% request trace anonymized. Jules already volunteered to share. We'll run two benchmark runs: (A) 7B batch6/50ms with KV cache, (B) 13B batch4/50ms with KV cache and current quant profile. We'll capture p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost per million tokens.
[06:10] Jules: Quick note — our traffic has diurnal spikes; would you run a sustained 24h to catch variability?
[06:15] Priya: Yes, 24h to capture diurnal is the plan. We'll push logs to the shared S3 bucket and provide the exact scripts.
[06:23] Marcus: If the benchmark shows 20% improvement on 7B with batching and caching we can probably stick with 7B; cheaper and simpler.
[06:29] Alex: Makes sense. Also one more idea: small quantization tweaks on 13B sometimes give disproportionate throughput gains with minimal quality loss. We'll include a quick ablation: q8 vs q4x for a subset of the model.
[06:41] Sam: Are there any vendor lock or licensing catches for switching quant levels?
[06:45] Alex: No vendor lock from Redwood's side. For some open models, license terms apply but switching quant doesn't change that. We'll flag any model-specific license notes.
[06:54] Raya: On dedicated pool costs — do you have a calculator for amortizing commit vs expected throughput?
[06:58] Alex: Yes, we'll update the cost sheet with a reserved capacity scenario — assumptions will include utilization bands (60/80/95%) so you can see per-token cost.
[07:07] Liam: I'll reattach the security pack and the SOC2 snippet after the call.
[07:11] Marcus: Anything else on the technical side?
[07:14] Priya: We'll add kernel selection notes, memory ladders, and the script we'll run. Also adding pointers for sticky routing to maximize cache hit rate.
[07:22] Alex: OK let's recap action items: Alex to run 24h microbenchmark (7B and 13B configs) and upload results by 4/17; Jules to send token dist and 1% trace by 4/16; Priya to prep kernel notes and quant ablation by 4/18; Raya to confirm VPC egress and regional test window by 4/20.
[07:40] Sam: That works. One last question — in the cost sheet, is network egress a big factor for you? It looked like you accounted 10% infra overhead, is that adjustable?
[07:49] Alex: Yes adjustable — if your network egress or support tiers change that will shift $/s. We'll parameterize it so you can toggle egress percentage.
[07:57] Marcus: Alright thanks everyone.
[08:00] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the benchmark link and updated cost sheet.
[08:05] Meeting end

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-hearings and shorthand; refer to shared sheet for numeric detail and named artifact links.
